title: Karna's abandonment
hook: the boy grows up worshipping the sun, and one morning a stranger asks him for the armor he was born in

segments.voice: Yesterday: a charioteer and his wife caught the basket downstream. Let go upstream, taken in downstream.

Every morning the young man stands facing the sun, hands joined, praying, until the sun is high and its heat is on his back. That's Karna, grown. He doesn't know the sun is his father. And the text adds a detail: while he prays, there's nothing he will refuse a Brahmin who asks. Today a stranger comes during that hour, and asks for the one thing Karna was born wearing.
screen: `HE FACES THE SUN EACH MORNING.` → `WHILE HE PRAYS, HE REFUSES NO BRAHMIN.` → `A STRANGER COMES.`

segments.voice: The stranger is dressed as a Brahmin, a priest. But the Mahabharata lets us in on the secret: he's Indra, king of the gods, and the father of Arjuna. Indra knows that as long as Karna wears his armor and earrings, nobody can beat him, so he comes to ask for them as alms. The Adi Parva tells this scene early, beside Karna's birth, though in the story's order it comes years later. In a later book, the sun himself warns Karna in a dream that Indra is coming, and tells him to refuse. Karna answers that he can't. He's given his word to give, and he'd rather lose his life than his name for giving. So the Brahmin asks. And Karna takes a blade, cuts the armor from his own body and the earrings from his ears, and hands them over. Indra, the text says, is pleased, and gives Karna a weapon in return, a dart that can kill one enemy. Now set this inside our story. Karna was abandoned once, set adrift by a mother who couldn't keep him. The armor was the one gift from his father that went with him. And today he gives it away with his own hands. The poem doesn't stop to call it wise or foolish. It shows the blade, and the gift: the boy who lost so much at the start of his life chooses to lose more, because someone asked.
screen: `A STRANGER: INDRA IN DISGUISE.` · `THE SUN WARNS HIM IN A DREAM.` · `HE CUTS THE ARMOR FROM HIS BODY.` · `A DART GIVEN IN RETURN.` · then, large: `HE GIVES BECAUSE SOMEONE ASKED.`

segments.voice: Turn toward whatever light is near you: a window, a lamp, the sun if it's out. Ask yourself quietly what you find hard to give, time, attention, forgiveness, something you own. Don't force an answer or promise anything; just hold the question in the light.
Karna's abandonment. The child set adrift grows into a man who gives away even his father's armor, cut from his own body, because someone asked.
Your line: he gives because someone asked. Even the armor he was born in. That's day seven hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: In Hindu storytelling Karna's name is tied to giving: his gift of the armor to Indra is retold as a picture of keeping one's word to give, whatever it costs.

fork.setup: you're Karna. you've been warned that a stranger will ask for the armor that keeps you safe. he's here, asking. what do you do?
options: refuse him, as the sun advised.
cut the armor from your body and give it.

original.note: Sanskrit kuṇḍala: an earring; Karna was born with his, and cut them off for Indra.

trapdoor: what you thought: Karna lost his armor in battle.
what it means: he gave it away himself, cutting it from his body for a stranger who asked during his prayers.
what a scholar hears: the Adi Parva gives the scene briefly; a later book tells it in full, with the sun's warning in a dream and Karna's refusal to break his word.

chat.says: Why would Karna give his armor to Indra, after the sun warned him?
options: He'd rather lose his life than his name for giving to whoever asked.
He never valued the armor, and was glad to be free of its weight.
Bhishma ordered him to, to keep the peace with the Pandavas.
chat.meaning: Warned by the sun in a dream, Karna still gave. He'd rather lose his life than his name for giving, so he cut the armor away.

Brahmin.meaning: a priest, of the priestly class

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, Arjuna's father

Arjuna.meaning: Pandu's third son, the archer, son of Indra

Adi Parva.meaning: the opening book of the Mahabharata

Karna.meaning: Kunti's firstborn, son of the sun, raised by a charioteer

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Karna's worship of the sun; Indra asks for the armor and earrings)
Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Kundalaharana Parva (the sun's warning in a dream; Karna gives the armor; Indra's dart)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the Adi Parva's description of Karna worshipping the sun until it heated his back, and that he refused nothing to Brahmins during that worship (the script now says 'a Brahmin', following the Adi Parva).
Confirm Indra's motive (to help Arjuna) and that the dart (shakti) can kill one enemy.
Confirm the Vana Parva dream warning from Surya and Karna's answer that he would rather lose his life than his fame/name for giving.
This scene happens later in the story's chronology than the tournament; it is placed here because the Adi Parva summarizes it within Karna's birth account. A Keeper may prefer to move it.
